title: Wildcards and Quoting
lead: Before a command runs, the shell expands wildcard patterns and treats spaces as separators. Select groups of files safely by using patterns and quotes correctly.
objectives: Distinguish brace expansion from glob expansion.
Explain how single quotes, double quotes and backslashes behave.
Check matching names before running a bulk operation.

sections.title: Wildcards: *, ? and []
body: The shell matches wildcard patterns against names in the current directory before running a command. `*` matches zero or more characters, while `?` matches exactly one. `img?.jpg` matches names with one character in that position; `img*.jpg` also includes longer names.
`[12]` matches exactly one of the characters in the brackets; `[0-9]` matches one digit. If nothing matches, Bash usually leaves the pattern unchanged. You can notice this in the command output.
The shell expands wildcards, not `ls`. When you run `ls *.txt`, the shell passes matching names to `ls` as separate arguments.

commands.where: When you want to inspect files with a particular extension together.
commands.why: You can see all matches without typing every name.

commands.what: Lists `.jpg` names with exactly one character after `img`.
commands.where: When a specific part and length of a name should match.
commands.why: `?` represents one character, so `img10.jpg` does not match.

commands.where: When only certain individual characters are allowed.
commands.why: It limits the pattern to characters inside the brackets.

commands.what: Expands the brace options into separate patterns.
commands.where: When you want to perform the same operation on multiple extensions.
commands.why: You can write similar patterns briefly and clearly.

sections.tip: If you are unsure what matches, first display the expansion with `printf '%s\n' *.jpg`. Do not run a command that changes files yet.

sections.title: Quotes and escaping
body: Quotes control how the shell interprets spaces and special characters. Without quotes, a name containing a space is split into multiple arguments. `"my file.txt"` keeps it together as one argument.

Characters inside single quotes stay literal; variables such as `$HOME` are not expanded. Double quotes preserve spaces but still expand variables and command substitutions. A backslash removes the special meaning of the character immediately after it.

commands.what: Passes a name containing a space as one argument.
commands.where: When listing names with spaces or passing them to commands.
commands.why: It prevents the shell from splitting the name into two parts.

commands.what: Prints the literal `$HOME` text inside single quotes.
commands.where: When you want to display special characters without expansion.
commands.why: You see the text as written, not the variable's value.

commands.what: Expands the variable inside double quotes and prints its value.
commands.where: When using a variable value while preserving spaces.
commands.why: The value stays together while the shell still expands the variable.

commands.what: Uses a backslash to remove the special meaning of the space.
commands.where: When you need to protect one special character.
commands.why: It keeps the name as one argument without using quotes.

sections.tip: When a filename contains a variable, usually quote it as `"$NAME"`; this also preserves any spaces in its value.

sections.title: Use wildcards safely
body: A wildcard pattern can match multiple names. Before a delete command such as `rm *.tmp`, run the same pattern with `ls` and check which names are selected.

In particular, `*` can match a broad set of names. First use `pwd` to confirm the current directory, then list the matches. Do not test an unfamiliar pattern with a destructive command on a real system.

commands.what: Shows matching names ending in `.tmp` before deletion.
commands.where: Immediately before a bulk operation using wildcards.
commands.why: You can confirm which names the command would affect.

commands.what: Asks for confirmation before deleting each matching file.
commands.where: When removing only temporary files you have checked.
commands.why: You get a chance to cancel if a match is wrong.

sections.warn: Never use wildcards in delete commands blindly. First confirm the directory and matches with `pwd` and `ls`; test destructive commands only in a safe environment.

sections.title: Apply patterns in practice tasks
body: This module uses English ASCII names such as `img1.jpg`, `img2.jpg`, `img10.png`, `doc1.txt` and `doc2.txt`. The command examples can be tried safely in the virtual lab.

Brace expansion is not the same as globbing: `{1,2}` is split into separate strings by the shell, while `*` and `?` match existing names. Predict which names a command receives, then verify in the lab.

commands.what: Prints matching names with the `.txt` extension.
commands.where: When testing a pattern before changing anything.
commands.why: You can see how the shell expands the pattern.

commands.what: Creates three separate names using brace options.
commands.where: When you need similar test names.
commands.why: It avoids repeating nearly identical commands.

sections.tip: Names containing spaces in the lab exist only in the virtual filesystem; you do not need to try the same commands on your real system.

t01.text: The lab is already set up with mixed names. Run `ls *.jpg` and observe that only names ending in `.jpg` are listed.
t01.hint: `*` matches zero or more characters; the dot and `jpg` suffix stay fixed in the pattern.

t02.text: Use `ls img?.jpg` to list `.jpg` names with exactly one character after `img`.
t02.hint: `?` matches exactly one character. Leave the pattern unquoted so the shell expands it.

t03.text: Use `ls doc*` to list names that start with `doc`.
t03.hint: `*` allows zero or more characters after `doc`.

t04.text: Run `echo *.txt`. How does the shell pass matching names to `echo`?
t04.hint: The shell first expands the pattern to matching names; `echo` prints those names.

t05.text: Use `ls img[12].jpg` to list images whose character after `img` is `1` or `2`.
t05.hint: Each option inside the brackets represents one character.

t06.text: Use `ls *.{jpg,png}` to match `.jpg` and `.png` names in one command.
t06.hint: The `jpg` and `png` brace options produce separate patterns.

t07.text: Create a `texts` directory and copy names that start with `doc` and end in `.txt` into it. Do not copy `notes.md`.

t08.text: Predict: does `echo '$HOME'` print the variable's value or the literal `$HOME` text? Run it to check.
t08.hint: Text inside single quotes is not expanded.

t09.text: Predict: what does `echo *.xyz` print if no names match `*.xyz`? Verify in the lab.
t09.hint: By default, Bash leaves an unmatched pattern unchanged.

t10.text: Debug: target the name `old report.txt` as one argument and remove that file.
t10.hint: Quote the name containing a space: `rm "old report.txt"`.

t11.text: Mini project: create a `backup` directory and copy only `.jpg` and `.png` files into it.

t12.text: Challenge: create the names `log_1.txt`, `log_2.txt` and `log_3.txt` with brace expansion, then remove all three with the `log_?` pattern.

t13.text: Ticket: Rename `my file.txt`, which contains a space, to `my_file.txt`. Make sure the original name stays one argument.

vm.intro: You can run the commands in this section in your own VM. Create files only inside `glob-lab` in your home directory; do not test wildcard deletions elsewhere.

v01.title: Single-character wildcard
v01.text: Create `glob-lab` in your home directory. Add the names `a1.txt` and `a2.txt` inside it, then list the `a?.txt` pattern.

blocks.cmd: mkdir -p ~/glob-lab && cd ~/glob-lab && touch a1.txt a2.txt && ls a?.txt

differs: `a?.txt` matches exactly one character; both names should appear.
If the names appear on one line, use `ls -1 a?.txt` to show each on its own line.

v02.title: Single and double quotes
v02.text: In the same terminal session, first set `NAME=linux`. Then print the variable with double quotes and with single quotes. The output should contain both `linux` and `$NAME`.
differs: If both lines show `linux`, you may have used double quotes instead of single quotes.
The `NAME=linux` assignment and `echo` commands must run in the same shell session.

v03.title: Preserve a name with spaces
v03.text: Create a directory named `my docs` inside `glob-lab`. Then list it with quotes; the output should contain `my docs`.

blocks.cmd: mkdir -p ~/glob-lab && cd ~/glob-lab && mkdir -p "my docs" && ls -d "my docs"

differs: If the name is split, check the quotes in both the creation and listing commands.
`ls -d` displays the directory name instead of its contents.

v04.title: Check matches before deleting
v04.text: Create two temporary files inside `glob-lab`. First list the `*.tmp` matches and confirm that only those two names appear. Delete them only if you confirmed the correct directory and matches.
differs: If other names appear, do not run the delete command; check `pwd` and the list first.
If there are no matches, confirm you are in `glob-lab` and that the names end in `.tmp`.

q1.explain: `?` represents exactly one character; `*` can match zero or more.

q2.q: Which form prints `$HOME` without expanding it?
q2.explain: Everything inside single quotes stays literal. In this example, a backslash also escapes the `$` character.

q3.q: In Bash, what does `echo *.xyz` do by default when no names match `*.xyz`?
q3.explain: By default, Bash passes an unmatched glob pattern to the command unchanged.

q4.q: How do you correctly list the name `my file.txt`?
q4.explain: The quotes preserve the space and pass the name to `ls` as one argument.

summary: `*` matches zero or more characters; `?` matches exactly one.
`[abc]` matches one of the listed characters; `{a,b}` expands options into separate strings.
Single quotes preserve everything literally; double quotes preserve spaces while expanding variables.
Protect names with spaces using quotes or a backslash.
Check the directory and matches before running a destructive command with wildcards.

glossary.meaning: A wildcard pattern that the shell matches against filenames.
A special character representing one or more characters in filename patterns.
Controlling how the shell interprets spaces and special characters.
A backslash (`\`) that removes the special meaning of the character after it.
